subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 14 periods = 560 minutes
Total: 14 periods · 9h 20min

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk, section 13.1 p.98
textbook_items_in_class.description: Decide which of the following are statistical questions: (a) price of a tennis ball in India; (b) ages of dogs on this street; (c) fraction of the class who like walking up a hill; (d) do you like reading; (e) approximately how many bricks are in this wall; (f) best bowler in yesterday's match; (g) last year's rainfall pattern in Barmer.

time_bands.activity: Open with the height-guessing scenario from the section: can you tell someone's gender from their height alone? Students share guesses aloud and the class notes that any single answer feels uncertain — different people give different heights, and the answer changes depending on the group you look at. This observation anchors the idea that some questions expect variation in their answers.

Introduce the statistical statement — a claim about a phenomenon expressed in numbers, proportions, or predictions — using the batting-consistency, cycling-time, and village-population examples from the section prose. Students identify what each statement claims and what data would be needed to check it. The class builds a working definition: a statistical question is one whose answer requires collecting and analysing data because the answer varies across individuals or times.

Math Talk, section 13.1 p.98 ("Decide which of the following are statistical questions: (a) price of a tennis ball....") Students work in pairs, classifying each question and writing one sentence of justification. Pairs share their reasoning; the class resolves disagreements by asking 'Would different people or places give different answers?'

Name statistics as the study of collecting, organising, analysing, interpreting, and presenting data. Students copy the five-word definition and volunteer one everyday statistical question from their own lives, briefly noting what data they would need to gather.

periods.teacher_notes: Watch for students who classify any numerical question as statistical — the key discriminator is whether variation in answers is expected, not simply whether numbers appear in the question. The price-of-a-tennis-ball example (a fixed, lookup answer) versus ages-of-dogs-on-this-street (varies by street and time) is the sharpest contrast to return to if confusion arises.

periods.activity_title: Arguing for and Against: Is This a Statistical Question?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk, section 13.1 p.98
textbook_items_in_class.description: Decide which of the following are statistical questions: (a) price of a tennis ball in India; (b) ages of dogs on this street; (c) fraction of the class who like walking up a hill; (d) do you like reading; (e) approximately how many bricks are in this wall; (f) best bowler in yesterday's match; (g) last year's rainfall pattern in Barmer.

time_bands.activity: Revisit the idea established in the opening unit — that statistical questions expect variation — by posing a borderline case: 'What is the most popular sport in our school?' Students debate in pairs whether this is statistical, surfacing the distinction between a single fixed fact and a question that requires surveying a population.

Return to Math Talk, section 13.1 p.98 ("Decide which of the following are statistical questions: (a) price of a tennis ball....") and focus on the contested items — particularly (e) approximately how many bricks in this wall and (f) best bowler in yesterday's match. Small groups construct written arguments for why each is or is not statistical, using the chapter's definition. Groups then share their reasoning, and the class adjudicates.

Students each pose two new questions: one that is definitively statistical and one that is definitively not. They swap with a neighbour, who must justify their classification in one or two sentences. The teacher circulates and selects two or three interesting boundary cases for a brief whole-class discussion.

Consolidate by having students write in their notebooks: 'A statistical question is different from a fixed-answer question because…' in their own words. Volunteers read aloud; the class refines the phrasing until it matches the chapter's definition precisely.

periods.teacher_notes: The richest reasoning moment comes when students argue about (e) — brick-counting — which looks numerical but has a fixed approximate answer, not genuine population variation. Encourage students to articulate the difference between estimation uncertainty and statistical variation; these are conceptually distinct and the chapter relies on that distinction going forward.

periods.activity_title: Fair Shares: Building the Arithmetic Mean

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 13.2 p.101
textbook_items_in_class.description: Shreyas bounces a ball on a bat with counts 6, 2, 9, 5, 4, 6, 3, 5 over 8 attempts; calculate the average number of bounces.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 13.2 p.101
textbook_items_in_class.description: Given weekly 100 m times for Nikhil (17, 18, 17, 16, 19, 17, 18) and Sunil (20, 18, 18, 17, 16, 16, 17), decide who on average ran quicker.

time_bands.activity: Use the cricket-scores comparison from the section: two players have different totals across different numbers of matches. The class proposes ways to compare them — highest score, total — and the teacher guides students to see that total alone misleads when match counts differ. The need for a per-match summary motivates the arithmetic mean.

Develop the mean as fair-share using the guava-sharing and daily-hibiscus-blooms examples from the section prose. Students work through: if guavas are redistributed equally, how many does each person get? They connect this to 'sum divided by count' and write the formula. The teacher notes the ancient Indian terms samamiti, samarajju, samīkaraṇa, and sāmya for the mean.

Figure it Out Q1, section 13.2 p.101 ("Shreyas bounces a ball on a bat with counts 6, 2, 9, 5, 4, 6, 3, 5 over 8 attempts....") Students compute the mean and then discuss: does the mean tell you Shreyas's best or most typical performance? Follow with Figure it Out Q4, section 13.2 p.101 ("Given weekly 100 m times for Nikhil… and Sunil….") Students compute both means and identify the quicker runner.

Figure it Out Q6, section 13.2 p.113 (if time permits) or verbal wrap-up: students state the mean of the six enrolment figures from Figure it Out Q5, section 13.2 p.101 ("Find the mean enrolment given six years' figures 1555, 1670, 1750, 2013, 2040, 2126....") if solved, and explain in one sentence why the mean is a useful single number to describe a dataset.

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent error is dividing by the number of distinct values rather than the total count of data points — when two entries share the same value, both still count separately. The Nikhil–Sunil comparison is a good check: both have seven values each, so the division is clean, and any error in the count stands out immediately.

periods.activity_title: Dot Plots, Range, and Reading the Spread

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 13.2 p.101
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the mean enrolment given six years' figures 1555, 1670, 1750, 2013, 2040, 2126.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 13.2 p.112
textbook_items_in_class.description: For Rintu's date-palm heights, fill the dot plot, mark the mean and median, describe the heights, find quicker ways to compute the mean, and count trees shorter than the average.

time_bands.activity: Using the onion-price data from Yahapur and Wahapur introduced in the section, define minimum, maximum, range, and average on the board. Students identify each for a short list of five values the teacher writes, building comfort with the vocabulary before applying it to a full dataset.

Demonstrate constructing a dot plot with the onion-price values: sort the values, draw a number line, and stack dots above repeated values. Students draw their own dot plot for Figure it Out Q5, section 13.2 p.101 ("Find the mean enrolment given six years' figures 1555, 1670, 1750, 2013, 2040, 2126....") on graph paper, marking the mean they computed.

Figure it Out Q3, section 13.2 p.112 ("For Rintu's date-palm heights, fill the dot plot, mark the mean and median, describe the heights, find quicker ways to compute the mean, and count trees shorter than the average....") Students work through the multi-part question, filling the dot plot, locating the mean, and discussing what the clustering of dots reveals about the palms.

Students write two observations about the date-palm dot plot: one about where values cluster and one about the range. Pairs share; the class agrees on which observations the dot plot genuinely supports versus which require extra information.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often compute the range by listing all values rather than subtracting minimum from maximum — reinforce the formula explicitly. When constructing dot plots, watch for students who space dots unevenly along the number line rather than placing them at their exact numerical positions; precise placement is essential for reading clustering correctly.

periods.activity_title: Median, Outliers, and When the Mean Misleads

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 13.2 p.112
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the median of the onion prices in Yahapur and in Wahapur.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 13.2 p.112
textbook_items_in_class.description: Given daily water-usage values, (a) decide whether the mean or median can lie between 25 and 30, justifying using their meaning; (b) decide whether either can be less than the minimum or greater than the maximum value.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the median using the family-height example from the section: sort the heights, locate the middle value, and note that for an even count the median is the mean of the two middle values. Students practise on two short datasets — one odd-count, one even-count — written on the board.

Figure it Out Q1, section 13.2 p.112 ("Find the median of the onion prices in Yahapur and in Wahapur....") Students sort both price lists and find the median of each. The teacher then introduces an outlier — a value that deviates greatly from the rest — using the short-story and newspaper-page examples, showing how a high outlier raises the mean above the median and a low outlier pulls it below.

Figure it Out Q4, section 13.2 p.112 ("Given daily water-usage values, (a) decide whether the mean or median can lie between 25 and 30….") Students work in pairs on both parts, writing justifications that use the definitions of mean and median rather than just computing. The zero-score versus did-not-play distinction from the section is discussed: only relevant values should be included in the count.

Class discussion: in what situations would you prefer to report the median over the mean? Students propose a real-life context (wages, house prices, test scores) and explain their choice. The teacher records the class's agreed-upon examples on the board alongside the chapter's definition of measures of central tendency.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common error with the median is forgetting to sort the data first — a few students will simply pick the middle item from the unsorted list. The zero-versus-absent distinction (a player scoring 0 versus not playing) is conceptually important; the section illustrates it with a mango tree's off-season months, and returning to that image helps students remember why the count in the denominator must match only the relevant observations.

periods.activity_title: Justifying Which Measure: Mean, Median, and Outliers

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 13.2 p.112
textbook_items_in_class.description: For Sanskruti's pet-count data (with some absent students), find the mean and median and describe the data.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 13.2 p.112
textbook_items_in_class.description: Fill a dot plot for the given newborn-baby weights of boys and girls, then analyse and compare the data.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 13.2 p.113
textbook_items_in_class.description: Given weights of sumo wrestlers and ballet dancers, estimate approximately how many times heavier a sumo wrestler is than a ballet dancer.

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out Q2, section 13.2 p.112 ("For Sanskruti's pet-count data (with some absent students), find the mean and median and describe the data....") Students handle the absent-students complication by deciding which values to include in the count, connecting to the zero-versus-absent principle established in earlier work on measures of central tendency.

Figure it Out Q5, section 13.2 p.112 ("Fill a dot plot for the given newborn-baby weights of boys and girls, then analyse and compare the data....") Students construct two dot plots side by side and compute mean and median for each group. They then write two sentences comparing the distributions, explicitly noting whether an outlier seems to be present and how it affects the mean.

Figure it Out Q7, section 13.2 p.113 ("Given weights of sumo wrestlers and ballet dancers, estimate approximately how many times heavier a sumo wrestler is than a ballet dancer....") Students reason about which representative value — mean or median — gives a fairer comparison when the two groups have very different spreads, and justify their choice in a short written argument.

Class synthesis: the teacher poses — 'If a dataset has a very high outlier, will the mean or median be larger? How do you know?' Students answer in one sentence and the class refines until the reasoning matches the section's explanation that a high outlier pulls the mean above the median.

periods.teacher_notes: In the pet-count question, students sometimes divide by the full class size even when some students were absent and their values are unknown — reinforce that the denominator must equal the number of data points actually collected. The sumo-vs-dancer question is a good vehicle for discussing when the mean is misleading: if one extreme value dominates, the median is more representative of the typical member of the group.

periods.activity_title: Comparing Groups: Heights, Estimates, and Variability

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 13.2 p.113
textbook_items_in_class.description: From the dot plots and central-tendency measures of another Grade 5 section, share observations and compare the heights of the two sections.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 13.2 p.101
textbook_items_in_class.description: Collect your own bounce data for 7 or more attempts and find the average.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 13.2 p.101
textbook_items_in_class.description: Track the number of flowers blooming each day over a week on a neighbourhood plant and find the average per day.

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out Q6, section 13.2 p.113 ("From the dot plots and central-tendency measures of another Grade 5 section, share observations and compare the heights of the two sections....") Students read the given dot plots and central-tendency values and write three specific observations that the data justifies, distinguishing these from claims the data does not support — connecting to the chapter's emphasis on variability and extremes alongside central tendency.

Figure it Out Q2, section 13.2 p.101 ("Collect your own bounce data for 7 or more attempts and find the average....") Students bounce a ball on a desk or floor for seven attempts, recording counts in their notebook, then compute the mean. The class pools results on the board to form a class dataset, giving a real dot plot to examine for clustering and spread.

Using the class dot plot constructed on the board, students find the median of the pooled bounce data and compare it to the mean. They discuss: does the class's combined dot plot look different from any individual's seven-attempt data? What does the spread of the class data tell us about variability in this task?

Brief consolidation: students write the minimum, maximum, range, mean, and median of the class's pooled bounce data in their notebooks, labelling each. This closes the section's core ideas — representative value, spread, and variability — as a unified set.

periods.teacher_notes: The live bounce activity creates genuine variation and student investment, but keep the data-collection phase tight so analysis gets sufficient time. A common reasoning error in Q6 is to compare dot-plot shapes visually without referencing numerical values — push students to cite specific numbers (a particular mean, a specific range) whenever they make a comparative claim.
materials: A rubber ball or similar bouncing object (one per pair or shared)

periods.activity_title: Building and Reading Double Bar Graphs

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 13.3 p.124
textbook_items_in_class.description: From the superpower-preference responses of Grade 5 and Grade 9, draw a double-bar graph comparing the two grades' choices with an appropriate scale.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 13.3 p.124
textbook_items_in_class.description: From the two-day temperature data for Jodhpur, draw a double-bar graph with scale 1 unit = 4°C and guess the two months.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the double (clustered) bar graph by combining the two single-column onion-price graphs — Yahapur and Wahapur — into one graph with bars placed side by side, as shown in section 13.3. Explain the two-step reading process: first identify what is given (organisation, scale, patterns) and then infer from what is given (analyse and interpret). Students note design choices: colour or pattern fills for greyscale readability, and the importance of a stated scale.

Figure it Out Q2, section 13.3 p.124 ("From the superpower-preference responses of Grade 5 and Grade 9, draw a double-bar graph comparing the two grades' choices with an appropriate scale....") Students choose a scale, draw the axes, label both bars for each superpower category with a key, and ensure bars for the two grades sit side by side.

Figure it Out Q3, section 13.3 p.124 ("From the two-day temperature data for Jodhpur, draw a double-bar graph with scale 1 unit = 4°C and guess the two months....") Students apply the prescribed scale, construct the graph, and then reason about what the temperature pattern suggests about the two months. They write one sentence guessing which months are represented and justifying with values from the graph.

Students exchange graphs with a neighbour and check: are the bars for the two groups placed side by side? Is the key present? Is the scale clearly labelled? Brief peer feedback is given verbally, and corrections are noted in pencil.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common construction error is drawing bars consecutively (as a single series) rather than clustered by category — a key and colour/pattern distinction must be present and consistent across all categories. When students guess the Jodhpur months, push them to reference specific temperature values from the graph rather than making impressionistic claims.
materials: Pencil and coloured pencils or pens

periods.activity_title: Interpreting Graphs: Rockets, Daylight, and Cricket

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 13.3 p.122
textbook_items_in_class.description: From an animal-speed infographic: (a) state the scale; (b) note what is interesting; (c) find a pair where one speed is about twice the other; (d) judge whether a sailfish is about 4 times faster than a humpback whale and the fastest aquatic animal.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 13.3 p.124–125
textbook_items_in_class.description: From the clustered-bar graph of electric-vehicle registrations: mark the Gujarat and Delhi bars from the table, describe changes 2022–2024, and answer comparison questions about several states.

time_bands.activity: Apply the two-step reading process — identify, then infer — to the rocket-launch data by organisation and year from the section. The teacher models: first state what the axes and scale show, then ask what the pattern suggests. Students see that time order is preserved for months but category order (organisations) is arbitrary.

Figure it Out Q1, section 13.3 p.122 ("From an animal-speed infographic: (a) state the scale; (b) note what is interesting; (c) find a pair where one speed is about twice the other; (d) judge whether a sailfish is about 4 times faster than a humpback whale....") Students work through all four parts, writing numerical justifications for (c) and (d).

Figure it Out Q4, section 13.3 p.124–125 ("From the clustered-bar graph of electric-vehicle registrations: mark the Gujarat and Delhi bars from the table, describe changes 2022–2024, and answer comparison questions....") Students mark the two missing bars, then answer the comparison questions, referencing bar heights and scale values explicitly.

Brief discussion of the Helsinki–Wellington daylight-hour graph from the section: why do their patterns appear inverted? Students explain in one sentence using the idea of opposite hemispheres and seasonal variation, demonstrating that a graph can reveal a geographic relationship without any additional text.

periods.teacher_notes: In the animal-speed infographic, students often answer part (d) by eye rather than by computation — insist on a written ratio or multiplication check. The EV-registration graph is a good place to discuss the section's point that design choices (colour versus pattern fills) affect readability when a graph is printed without colour; ask students how they would distinguish the bars if they could only use shading.

periods.activity_title: What Does the Graph Really Tell Us?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 13.3 p.124–125
textbook_items_in_class.description: From the clustered-bar graph of electric-vehicle registrations: mark the Gujarat and Delhi bars from the table, describe changes 2022–2024, and answer comparison questions about several states.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 13.3 p.124
textbook_items_in_class.description: From the superpower-preference responses of Grade 5 and Grade 9, draw a double-bar graph comparing the two grades' choices with an appropriate scale.

time_bands.activity: Return to the cricket runs-per-over double bar graph with wicket markers from the section. Students identify what is given (two innings, over-by-over runs, wicket markers) and then infer: who batted first, where wickets fell, and what the target was. This models the two-step identify-and-infer process as a structured argument.

Revisit the EV-registration graph from Figure it Out Q4, section 13.3 p.124–125 ("From the clustered-bar graph of electric-vehicle registrations: mark the Gujarat and Delhi bars from the table, describe changes 2022–2024....") Focus on the reasoning sub-questions: students must now justify comparative statements ('State X grew faster than State Y between 2022 and 2024') using specific bar-height values and differences.

Students revisit their superpower-preference double bar graphs from Figure it Out Q2, section 13.3 p.124 ("From the superpower-preference responses of Grade 5 and Grade 9, draw a double-bar graph....") and write three statements: one that their graph directly supports, one that requires inference, and one that their graph does NOT support. Pairs swap and critique each other's statements for validity.

Class discussion: what is the difference between reading a value off a graph and making an inference from a graph? Students propose a one-sentence rule for when a graph-based claim counts as justified, which the teacher records on the board as a shared norm for the remaining units.

periods.teacher_notes: The core reasoning skill here is separating what a graph directly shows from what it implies — students often treat a visual impression (one bar looks 'much taller') as evidence without citing the underlying numbers. Encourage the habit of writing the actual values read off the scale whenever making a comparative claim; this is the chapter's model for data-based argument.
materials: Student-constructed graphs from the previous unit

periods.activity_title: Which Claims Does the Data Justify?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 13.4 p.129
textbook_items_in_class.description: From the pocket-count dot plots for boys and girls, decide which statements about variability, median, mean, and maximum are true.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 13.4 p.129–130
textbook_items_in_class.description: From a table of points over four games with a 'did not play' entry: (a) find A's average per game; (b) decide whether to divide C's and B's totals by 3 or 4 and why; (c) decide who is the best performer.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 13.4 p.130
textbook_items_in_class.description: Compare two groups' General Knowledge quiz scores using mean and median and describe their performance.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the Data Detective framework from section 13.4: comparing heights across grades and schools, and examining the 1989–2019 Indian height survey, the class discusses what kinds of statements a dataset can and cannot support. The teacher writes three sample statements on the board — one justified, one unjustified, one requiring extrapolation — and students label each, giving reasons.

Figure it Out Q1, section 13.4 p.129 ("From the pocket-count dot plots for boys and girls, decide which statements about variability, median, mean, and maximum are true....") Students examine each statement and write 'true', 'false', or 'cannot be determined', with a one-phrase justification citing the dot plot's numerical features.

Figure it Out Q2, section 13.4 p.129–130 ("From a table of points over four games with a 'did not play' entry….") Students resolve the did-not-play ambiguity by applying the zero-versus-absent principle — only the games actually played count in the denominator — then compare averages to decide the best performer, writing a brief justification.

Figure it Out Q3, section 13.4 p.130 ("Compare two groups' General Knowledge quiz scores using mean and median....") Students compute both measures and write a short comparative description, practising the Data Detective habit of grounding every claim in a numerical value from the data.

periods.teacher_notes: The 'did not play' problem in Q2 is the most conceptually demanding item: students who simply divide totals by 4 are penalising a player for not playing — the chapter explicitly cautions against this, and the mango-tree analogy from section 13.2 is worth invoking again. In Q1, push students to distinguish between 'the dot plot shows' and 'the dot plot implies'; this is the core Data Detective skill the section is building.

periods.activity_title: Trends, Extrapolation, and the Limits of a Sample

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 13.4 p.130
textbook_items_in_class.description: Two 7th-grade sections each have 15 boys and 15 girls; given one section's mean height is 154.2 cm, choose what must be true about the other section's mean.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 13.4 p.131
textbook_items_in_class.description: From a skyscraper infographic: (a) estimate the number of skyscrapers in New York, Tokyo, and London; (b) judge the validity of statements about cities relative to Mumbai and the world's tallest building.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 13.4 p.130
textbook_items_in_class.description: For 17 students' heights, suggest a threshold height that splits the class into two equal groups, and estimate their age from the 'Telling Tall Tales' table.

time_bands.activity: Using the 1989–2019 Indian height survey from section 13.4, the teacher poses: 'Which successive ages show the greatest growth for boys? For girls?' Students identify the relevant rows, compute differences, and state their finding with the values. The teacher then asks: 'What would we predict for 2029?' — introducing extrapolation and its limits, particularly the section's caution that one or two schools' data cannot generalise to a whole country.

Figure it Out Q7, section 13.4 p.130 ("Two 7th-grade sections each have 15 boys and 15 girls; given one section's mean height is 154.2 cm, choose what must be true about the other section's mean....") Students reason about what the given mean implies — and does not imply — about the second section, using the definition of mean to test each option logically.

Figure it Out Q8, section 13.4 p.131 ("From a skyscraper infographic: (a) estimate the number of skyscrapers in New York, Tokyo, and London; (b) judge the validity of statements....") Students read bar values, estimate carefully, and then evaluate each validity statement — marking it as 'supported', 'not supported', or 'partially supported', with a numerical reason.

Figure it Out Q5, section 13.4 p.130 ("For 17 students' heights, suggest a threshold height that splits the class into two equal groups….") Students sort the 17 heights and identify the median as a natural splitting point, then consult the Telling Tall Tales table to estimate age, writing one sentence connecting the threshold to the concept of median as the central divider.

periods.teacher_notes: Q7 is a deductive exercise in the meaning of the mean: the mean of the combined group is the average of all 30 values, which does not fix the second section's mean at any particular value — students who think it must equal 154.2 cm are confusing mean of means with the overall mean. The section's caution about generalising from a small sample to a country is worth stating explicitly: conclusions about 'all Indian children' require far more than a few classrooms' data.

periods.activity_title: Constructing Graphs and Analysing Real Datasets

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 13.4 p.130
textbook_items_in_class.description: From survey data of watching vs participating in five sports, choose a scale, draw a double-bar graph, and write observations.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q10, section 13.4 p.132
textbook_items_in_class.description: For Aditi's Sudoku-solving times over two weeks: (a) construct a dot plot for both weeks; (b) describe the mean, median, and observations.

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out Q4, section 13.4 p.130 ("From survey data of watching vs participating in five sports, choose a scale, draw a double-bar graph, and write observations....") Students select an appropriate scale, construct the graph with a key distinguishing watching and participating, and then write two data-justified observations — one about which sport shows the largest gap between watching and participating, and one about an overall pattern.

Figure it Out Q10, section 13.4 p.132 ("For Aditi's Sudoku-solving times over two weeks: (a) construct a dot plot for both weeks; (b) describe the mean, median, and observations....") Students construct both dot plots on the same number line for ease of comparison, compute mean and median for each week, and write a short comparative description addressing whether Aditi improved, considering both central tendency and spread.

Students exchange completed graphs with a partner for a quick check: is the scale consistent? Are both groups labelled? Does the written observation cite a value from the graph rather than just an impression? Verbal feedback is exchanged, and students note one correction to make.

periods.teacher_notes: In Q4, students often choose a scale that makes bars either too tall or too short — remind them that the tallest bar should comfortably reach roughly three-quarters of the graph's height, which helps them judge an appropriate scale unit. In Q10, watch for students who compute the mean of week 2 without accounting for all seven values; the dot plot they construct is a useful self-check since each data point should appear as a dot.
materials: Pencil and coloured pencils or pens

periods.activity_title: Data Collection, Dot Plots, and Number-Lock Deduction

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 13.4 p.130
textbook_items_in_class.description: Describe the mean and median of your class's heights, visualising them on a dot plot.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q9, section 13.4 p.131
textbook_items_in_class.description: Estimate and then measure the listed objects, draw a double-bar graph, and find the average difference between estimated and measured values.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q13, section 13.4 p.133
textbook_items_in_class.description: Small-group project: either 'Our heights vs. our family's heights' (dot plot and double-bar graph of student and family heights) or 'Estimating time' (dot plots and double-bar graph of 1-minute and 3-minute estimates), then pool and analyse everyone's data.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q11, section 13.4 p.132–133
homework.description: Individual project: either 'How Long is a Sentence?' (dot-plot sentence lengths from two textbook pages and compare with mean/median) or 'What is in a Name?' (mean/median name length, popular starting letters, median starting letter, and a double-bar graph of vowel/consonant patterns).

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out Q6, section 13.4 p.130 ("Describe the mean and median of your class's heights, visualising them on a dot plot....") Each student records their own height on a sticky note or calls it out; the class constructs a shared dot plot on the board. Students compute the class mean and median collaboratively, then write one sentence about where the central value sits relative to the spread.

Figure it Out Q9, section 13.4 p.131 ("Estimate and then measure the listed objects, draw a double-bar graph, and find the average difference between estimated and measured values....") Students estimate each object's length first, then measure with a ruler, recording both values. They draft a double-bar graph comparing estimated versus measured, and compute the average absolute difference to quantify their estimation accuracy.

Figure it Out Q13, section 13.4 p.133 ("Small-group project: either 'Our heights vs. our family's heights' or 'Estimating time'….") Groups choose one option. For 'Estimating time', each student estimates one minute silently and records their count; the group pools data, constructs a dot plot, and computes mean and median. The group writes two sentences on what the data reveals about their collective sense of a minute.

Close with the number-lock deduction puzzle from section 13.4: the teacher poses the puzzle clues aloud and students work individually to deduce the combination, then share their reasoning. This playful closing reinforces the chapter's Data Detective spirit — using given constraints systematically to arrive at a unique conclusion.

periods.teacher_notes: The class dot plot in Q6 works best if heights are called out in ascending order so placement is quick; if time is short, have students place their values in groups of five and label each group's range. The estimation-and-measurement activity in Q9 is strongest when students commit to their estimates before picking up a ruler — any adjustment after measuring defeats the purpose of quantifying estimation error.
materials: Pencil and coloured pencils or pens
Sticky notes (optional, for class dot plot)

items.prompt: Which of the following is a statistical question?

options.label: A
options.text: What is the price of a litre of milk in India today?

options.label: B
options.text: How many hours of sleep do Grade 7 students in our school get each night?

options.label: C
options.text: How many legs does a spider have?

options.label: D
options.text: What is the capital of Rajasthan?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: How many hours of sleep do Grade 7 students in our school get each night? — because this question expects different answers from different students and requires collecting and analysing data.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the definition: a statistical question is one whose answer varies across individuals or times and so requires data collection and analysis.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may be confusing a numerical lookup question (a single fixed price) with a statistical question; the price of milk on a given day is a fixed fact, not a question that produces variation across a population.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may think any science-related question is statistical; spider legs is a fixed biological fact with no variation across respondents.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may be confused about the role of data; the capital of a state is a single fixed answer requiring no data collection.

inclusivity.support: Revisit the definition in section 13.1: a statistical question expects variation in answers across people or times.
inclusivity.challenge: Write one more statistical question and one more non-statistical question, then explain in your own words what makes each what it is.

items.prompt: A student practises throwing a ball into a basket. Over six attempts she scores the following number of successful throws: 3, 7, 5, 4, 6, 5. Calculate the arithmetic mean (average) number of successful throws per attempt.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the arithmetic mean formula: sum all values and divide by the count of values.

inclusivity.support: Draw six boxes representing the six attempts and write each value; add all the numbers and then share them equally among six boxes.
inclusivity.challenge: What single value would you need to replace one of the six scores with so that the new mean is 6? Show your working.

items.prompt: A school library records the number of books borrowed each day for five days: 12, 18, 15, 21, 9. Calculate the mean number of books borrowed per day.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Sum all five daily values and divide by 5 to find the arithmetic mean.

inclusivity.support: Write out the addition step by step: 12 + 18 = 30, 30 + 15 = 45, and so on before dividing.
inclusivity.challenge: The library wants the mean to reach 17 books per day over six days. How many books must be borrowed on the sixth day?

items.prompt: The prices (in rupees per kilogram) of tomatoes recorded on seven days in a market are: 22, 25, 20, 28, 24, 23, 26. Sort the values and find the median price.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Sorted: 20, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 28. There are 7 values, so the median is the 4th value = 24 rupees per kilogram.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Sort the data in ascending order and identify the middle value (position (7+1)/2 = 4th) as the median.

inclusivity.support: Write the seven numbers in a line from smallest to largest and count inward from both ends to find the middle one.
inclusivity.challenge: An eighth day's price of 40 rupees is added. Find the new median. Does the mean change more than the median? Show why.

items.prompt: A double bar graph shows the number of students who prefer cricket versus football in Grade 6 and Grade 7. In Grade 6, cricket: 18, football: 12. In Grade 7, cricket: 14, football: 20. A student says, 'Football is more popular overall across both grades.' Is this statement supported by the data? Explain using the values.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Total cricket across both grades = 18 + 14 = 32. Total football = 12 + 20 = 32. The totals are equal, so the statement that football is more popular overall is NOT supported — the two sports are equally popular across both grades combined.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Sum each sport's values across both grades and compare the totals to evaluate the claim.

inclusivity.support: Add each sport's numbers for Grade 6 and Grade 7 separately, then compare the two sums.
inclusivity.challenge: Write one statement that the data does support, and one that it does not support but would require more information to verify.

items.prompt: A bar in an animal-speed infographic reaches the 72 km/h mark on a scale where each grid unit represents 10 km/h. Another bar reaches 36 km/h. Is one animal's speed approximately twice the other's? Show your reasoning with the values.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 72 ÷ 36 = 2. Yes, the first animal's speed is exactly twice the second animal's speed, so the statement is supported.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Read the two speeds from the stated bar heights and compute the ratio to check the 'twice' claim.

inclusivity.support: Double the smaller speed (36 × 2) and check whether the result equals the larger speed.
inclusivity.challenge: If the scale changed to 1 unit = 8 km/h and the same two bars span 9 units and 4.5 units respectively, would the 'twice' relationship still hold? Explain.

items.prompt: A survey records how many students watch cricket versus play cricket in five different classes. The data is: watch — 30, 25, 28, 32, 20; play — 10, 15, 12, 8, 18. Calculate the mean number of students who watch cricket and the mean number who play cricket across the five classes.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Mean (watch) = (30 + 25 + 28 + 32 + 20) ÷ 5 = 135 ÷ 5 = 27. Mean (play) = (10 + 15 + 12 + 8 + 18) ÷ 5 = 63 ÷ 5 = 12.6. On average, 27 students watch cricket and 12.6 students play cricket per class.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Sum each column separately and divide each total by 5 to find the respective means.

inclusivity.support: Add the 'Watch' column first, write the total, then divide by 5; repeat for the 'Play' column.
inclusivity.challenge: Suppose a sixth class has 24 watchers and 14 players. Recompute both means for six classes and describe how each mean changed.

items.prompt: The heights (in cm) of 9 students in a class are: 142, 148, 151, 145, 160, 147, 153, 149, 155. Find the median height and the mean height. Round the mean to one decimal place.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Sort the nine values to find the middle (5th) value as the median; sum all nine and divide by 9 for the mean.

inclusivity.support: Write the heights from smallest to largest and count to the 5th value for the median before computing the sum for the mean.
inclusivity.challenge: The value 160 cm is an outlier. Remove it and recompute both the mean and median for the remaining 8 students. Which measure changed more, and why?

items.prompt: Priya says: 'How many books does each student in our class own?' is a statistical question because the answer involves numbers. Rahim says it is not a statistical question because each student has a fixed number of books. Who is correct, and why? Use the definition of a statistical question in your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Priya is correct. A statistical question is one whose answer is expected to vary across individuals and therefore requires collecting and analysing data. Different students own different numbers of books, so the answer varies across the class — that variation is precisely what makes it statistical. Rahim's reasoning is flawed: each student does have a fixed number, but the question asks about the class as a group, and the answers differ across people.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the definition: a question is statistical if its answer varies across individuals or times and requires data collection to answer.

inclusivity.support: Think aloud with a partner: if you asked five friends how many books they own, would you expect all five to give the same answer?
inclusivity.challenge: Rephrase the question so that it becomes non-statistical, and explain what you changed and why that change matters.

items.prompt: A teacher records how many pets five students have: 0, 1, 0, 2, 12. She finds the mean is 3 and the median is 1. Explain why the median is a better representative value for this dataset than the mean. Use the terms 'outlier' and 'central tendency' in your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The value 12 is an outlier — it deviates greatly from the other values, which are all 0, 1, or 2. The mean of 3 is pulled upward by this outlier, so it lies above four of the five values and does not reflect where most of the data sits. The median of 1, being the middle value of sorted data, is not affected by the outlier and better captures the central tendency — the point around which most values cluster. So the median is more representative here.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the outlier, explain how it inflates the mean above the median, and use the definition of central tendency to justify the median's representativeness.

inclusivity.support: Talk through it with a partner: does a mean of 3 feel like a typical number of pets for this group? Why or why not?
inclusivity.challenge: What single value could you add to this dataset so that the mean and median are equal? Show your working.

items.prompt: Two classes each have seven students. Class A heights (cm): 140, 142, 143, 145, 147, 148, 150. Class B heights (cm): 130, 138, 143, 145, 147, 155, 167. Both classes have the same median (145 cm). A student claims the two classes are equally tall on average. Do you agree? Use the mean and range of both classes to support your argument.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Class A mean = (140+142+143+145+147+148+150) ÷ 7 = 1015 ÷ 7 = 145 cm. Class B mean = (130+138+143+145+147+155+167) ÷ 7 = 1025 ÷ 7 ≈ 146.4 cm. Class A range = 150 − 140 = 10 cm. Class B range = 167 − 130 = 37 cm. The means differ slightly (145 vs 146.4 cm), so they are not exactly equally tall on average. More importantly, Class B has a much greater range (37 cm vs 10 cm), meaning its heights are far more spread out, even though the medians are the same. The student's claim is incorrect: equal medians do not imply equal averages or equal spread.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute the mean and range for each class, then compare both measures to evaluate the claim about equal average height.

inclusivity.support: Compute each class's mean step by step, then subtract the smallest height from the largest for the range before comparing.
inclusivity.challenge: Construct a dot plot for each class side by side and explain in one additional sentence what the visual representation reveals that the numbers alone do not.

items.prompt: A double bar graph shows electric-vehicle registrations (in thousands) for two states across three years. State X: 2022 → 8, 2023 → 14, 2024 → 22. State Y: 2022 → 20, 2023 → 22, 2024 → 25. A student claims State X is growing faster than State Y. Justify or refute this claim using values from the data.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: State X increased from 8 to 22 thousand over two years, a rise of 14 thousand (an increase of 175%). State Y increased from 20 to 25 thousand, a rise of only 5 thousand (an increase of 25%). In absolute terms, State X added 14 thousand registrations versus State Y's 5 thousand. In relative terms, State X grew far more rapidly. The claim is justified: State X is growing faster than State Y.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute the increase (2024 minus 2022) for each state and compare absolute and proportional growth to evaluate the claim.

inclusivity.support: Subtract the 2022 value from the 2024 value for each state and compare the two differences before drawing a conclusion.
inclusivity.challenge: If growth continues at the same absolute rate, in which year will State X first exceed State Y? Show the calculation.

items.prompt: In a game played over four rounds, Player A scores 5, 8, 6, 7. Player B scores 9, 11, and 'did not play' in round 3, and 10 in round 4. A student calculates B's average by dividing her total by 4. Explain whether this is correct, and state what B's correct average per game is.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Round | Player A | Player B |
| 1 | 5 | 9 |
| 2 | 8 | 11 |
| 3 | 6 | did not play |
| 4 | 7 | 10 |

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The student's calculation is incorrect. Player B did not play in round 3, so that round contributes no score and should not be counted in the denominator. Only the three rounds B actually played are relevant. B's total = 9 + 11 + 10 = 30. B's average = 30 ÷ 3 = 10 points per game played.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the principle that only the rounds actually played count in the denominator — a 'did not play' entry is not a zero score.

inclusivity.support: Recall the mango-tree example from the chapter: off-season months where no mangoes grow should not be counted when computing the average monthly yield for the flowering season.
inclusivity.challenge: If B had scored 0 in round 3 instead of not playing, what would her average be? Explain how this is different from the 'did not play' case.

items.prompt: Section A of Grade 7 has 15 boys and 15 girls. The mean height of all 30 students in Section A is 154.2 cm. A student says: 'Therefore, the mean height of the 30 students in Section B must also be 154.2 cm.' Explain whether this conclusion can be drawn from the given information.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The conclusion cannot be drawn. Knowing Section A's mean height tells us nothing about Section B's heights — the two sections are independent groups, and their means are determined by their own individual values. Section B's mean could be higher, lower, or coincidentally equal to 154.2 cm; the given information provides no basis for any claim about Section B.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Reason that the mean of one group fixes only the sum of that group's values and gives no information about a separate, independent group.

inclusivity.support: Think about it this way: if you knew the average age of people in one room, would that tell you the average age of people in a different room?
inclusivity.challenge: What additional information would you need about Section B to say something meaningful about its mean height? Describe it precisely.
